title: The cut hair
hookLine: at the river Anoma he cuts his hair with his sword and puts on a simple robe

cards: By dawn, the three riders reach a river. The later telling names it the Anoma.
The prince gets down from Kanthaka on the sandy bank, still dressed as what he was: a prince in silk and jewels, his long hair bound up in a royal topknot.

People sometimes cut their hair after something ends, a breakup, a new job, a hard year, and the mirror shows someone lighter, someone starting over. Hair can carry who we've been. The prince draws his sword.

teach.b: He takes his long hair in one hand and cuts through it with the sword.

In the telling, what's left is short, curling to the right, and it stays that length for the rest of his life; tradition links this to the small tight curls on statues of the Buddha. He throws the topknot into the air.
He takes off his royal clothes, puts on a simple robe the color of earth, like the wanderer from the fourth sight, and gives his jewels to Channa to take home. In that moment, the prince is gone.
There's a samana on the riverbank.
The word for this is pabbajja, going forth: leaving the household life for the homeless one. It's still the word for it.
In Theravada communities, when someone becomes a novice monk or nun, the ceremony is called pabbajja, and the head is shaved, as on that riverbank.

teach.h: BOYS DRESSED AS PRINCES, THEN ROBED.
teach.b: In Myanmar, there's a ceremony for boys called shinbyu: first they're dressed up as princes, in silk and makeup, and paraded through town, then their heads are shaved and they put on robes for a time, retelling this very morning with their own lives.

What pabbajja teaches, even for people who never shave a head, is that some things we carry are costumes. The prince didn't hate his hair or his jewels. He just didn't need them for where he was going.
There was simply less to carry.

how: In Theravada novice ordination, called pabbajja, the head is shaved and a robe put on; in Myanmar, boys going through shinbyu are dressed as princes before being robed as novices for a time.

o: the robe a monk receives at full ordination
leaving home life to become a wandering seeker
a pilgrimage to the river where the Buddha bathed

games.q: what's inside the going forth — tap the pairs.
p: boys dressed as princes, then robed

s: tradition links the Buddha's curls in statues to the story of the cut hair
in the telling, his hair stayed short and curled to the right for life.
pabbajja is only a word from the old stories
it's still the name of novice ordination, with the head shaved.
the prince cut his hair because he hated his old life
he didn't need it where he was going. less to carry.

games.q: you're on the riverbank at dawn, still in silk and jewels, a sword at your side. what do you do?
o: cut off your hair with the sword and put on a plain robe.
ride back to the palace before anyone wakes.
sell the jewels to fund the journey.
games.why: he cuts his hair, throws the topknot into the air, and trades silk for an earth-colored robe. the prince is gone; a samana stands on the bank.

practice: Think of one small vanity you carry, with no need for shame about it: checking your reflection, a way you need to look before leaving the house, a number you check, likes or steps or followers.
Picture setting it down on a riverbank, just for today, the way the prince set down his jewels, and notice what changes, if anything, without it. Then rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Pabbajja. Going forth: leaving home life for the homeless one. Today, it's the name of the ceremony where a novice's head is shaved.

orig.note: Pali: going forth, leaving home life; the novice ordination. Sanskrit pravrajyā.

carryVoice: Your line: less to carry. A prince rode to the river, and a samana walked on. Thirty-nine days in.

sources.ref: Nidanakatha (introduction to the Jataka): the cutting of the hair at the river Anoma
